lines.act: ACT ONE — Trapping the circle
lines.text: People knew pi roughly long before anyone could explain it, because they measured it.

lines.act: ACT ONE — Trapping the circle
lines.text: Babylonian scribes usually just used three, and one clay tablet uses three and one eighth.

lines.act: ACT ONE — Trapping the circle
lines.text: In Egypt, the Rhind papyrus, copied around sixteen fifty BC, finds the area of a round field in a way that works out to about three point one six.

lines.act: ACT ONE — Trapping the circle
lines.text: These numbers were good enough for fields and granaries. But they were measurements, not reasons. Nobody could say why the number was what it was.

lines.act: ACT ONE — Trapping the circle
lines.text: The first person to go after the question systematically was Archimedes, in Syracuse, in the third century BC.

lines.act: ACT ONE — Trapping the circle
lines.text: His problem is easy to state. You can't lay a straight ruler along a curve and read off its length.

lines.act: ACT ONE — Trapping the circle
lines.text: But you can do this. Draw a polygon inside the circle. Its perimeter is a little shorter than the circle.

lines.act: ACT ONE — Trapping the circle
lines.text: Then draw a polygon outside, hugging the circle. Its perimeter is a little longer.

lines.act: ACT ONE — Trapping the circle
lines.text: So the circle, which you cannot measure directly, is trapped between two numbers that you can.

lines.act: ACT ONE — Trapping the circle
lines.text: Archimedes started with hexagons, six sides each, and got a rough squeeze, somewhere between three and about three point four six.

lines.act: ACT ONE — Trapping the circle
lines.text: Then he doubled the sides. Twelve. Twenty-four. Forty-eight. Ninety-six.

lines.act: ACT ONE — Trapping the circle
lines.text: With every doubling, the polygons hug the circle a little tighter, and the gap between them shrinks.

lines.act: ACT ONE — Trapping the circle
lines.text: At ninety-six sides, he proved that pi lies between three point one four zero eight and three point one four two nine.

lines.act: ACT ONE — Trapping the circle
lines.text: That upper bound is twenty-two over seven, the very fraction many of us still use today.

lines.act: ACT ONE — Trapping the circle
lines.text: The same idea was found again, independently, in China.

lines.act: ACT ONE — Trapping the circle
lines.text: In the fifth century, Zu Chongzhi went all the way to a polygon with twelve thousand two hundred and eighty-eight sides, and pinned pi down to seven decimal places.

lines.act: ACT ONE — Trapping the circle
lines.text: He also gave the fraction three hundred and fifty-five over one hundred and thirteen, which is right to six decimal places.

lines.act: ACT ONE — Trapping the circle
lines.text: In Europe, Archimedes' squeeze stayed the method of choice for almost nineteen hundred years.

lines.act: ACT ONE — Trapping the circle
lines.text: As late as sixteen ten, Ludolph van Ceulen was still doubling polygons, out to a shape with more than four quintillion sides, and he got thirty-five digits.

lines.act: ACT ONE — Trapping the circle
lines.text: They were carved on his tombstone, and for a long time German speakers called pi the Ludolphine number.

lines.act: ACT ONE — Trapping the circle
lines.text: But the real gift of Archimedes isn't the digits. It's what his method shows pi to be.

lines.act: ACT ONE — Trapping the circle
lines.text: Pi is the end of a process. It is where those polygons are heading as their sides grow without limit.

lines.act: ACT ONE — Trapping the circle
lines.text: In other words, pi lives right on the border between straight and curved.

lines.act: ACT ONE — Trapping the circle
lines.text: It is the price you pay to turn something with corners into something perfectly smooth.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Pi is about turning
lines.text: Now for the most important part.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Pi is about turning
lines.text: In school, pi arrives as a fact about circles, so it's natural to think pi is about circles.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Pi is about turning
lines.text: It isn't, really. Pi is about turning.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Pi is about turning
lines.text: To see why, we need a unit of angle that most of us met once, briefly, and then forgot. The radian.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Pi is about turning
lines.text: We usually measure angles in degrees, and a full turn is three hundred and sixty of them.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Pi is about turning
lines.text: But there's nothing mathematical about three hundred and sixty. Somebody chose it.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Pi is about turning
lines.text: It most likely comes from Babylonian astronomy, which counted in sixties.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Pi is about turning
lines.text: Three hundred and sixty can be divided evenly in twenty-four different ways, and it's close to the number of days in a year.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Pi is about turning
lines.text: Very handy. But still, a convention.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Pi is about turning
lines.text: A radian is different, because nobody had to pick a number.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Pi is about turning
lines.text: Take a circle whose radius is one. Walk along its edge a distance of exactly one radius.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Pi is about turning
lines.text: The angle you've swept out from the centre is one radian, a little over fifty-seven degrees. That's the whole definition.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Pi is about turning
lines.text: And this is where pi steps in. A circle of radius one has a circumference of two pi.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Pi is about turning
lines.text: So a full turn is two pi radians. Half a turn is pi. A quarter turn is pi over two.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Pi is about turning
lines.text: So pi isn't some number that just happens to pop out when you measure circles.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Pi is about turning
lines.text: Pi is how far you travel along the edge when you turn halfway round a circle of radius one. It is the natural measure of half a turn.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Pi is about turning
lines.text: Some mathematicians even argue that the real constant should be the full turn, two pi, which they call tau.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Pi is about turning
lines.text: Either way, it is a story about turning.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Pi is about turning
lines.text: Look at pi this way, and it starts showing up in places with no circles at all.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Pi is about turning
lines.text: Imagine a point running steadily around a circle, and look only at its shadow on a wall.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Pi is about turning
lines.text: The shadow just slides up and down, up and down. Trace it out over time, and you get a wave. A sine wave.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Pi is about turning
lines.text: That is exactly how a pendulum swings, at least for small swings, and it's why the formula for its period has a two pi in it.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Pi is about turning
lines.text: A sound wave is air pressure rising and falling in that same rhythm.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Pi is about turning
lines.text: And the alternating current in your walls is made by a coil spinning inside a generator.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Pi is about turning
lines.text: Wherever something repeats, there is a hidden turn behind it, and pi comes along to measure it.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Pi is about turning
lines.text: The circle is just the easiest picture of a turn to see. It isn't where pi comes from.

lines.act: ACT THREE — Why pi never ends
lines.text: Pi is irrational. That means you cannot write it as one whole number divided by another.

lines.act: ACT THREE — Why pi never ends
lines.text: To see why that matters, look at what fractions do.

lines.act: ACT THREE — Why pi never ends
lines.text: Divide one by three, and you get zero point three three three, repeating forever. A tiny bar over the three writes it down completely.

lines.act: ACT THREE — Why pi never ends
lines.text: Divide one by seven, and you get one four two eight five seven, then one four two eight five seven again, and again.

lines.act: ACT THREE — Why pi never ends
lines.text: That isn't luck. Each step of the division leaves a remainder, and unless the division comes out exactly, there are only six remainders it can be.

lines.act: ACT THREE — Why pi never ends
lines.text: So within six steps, some remainder has to come back, and from that moment, the digits repeat.

lines.act: ACT THREE — Why pi never ends
lines.text: Every fraction behaves like this. Its digits either stop, or they fall into a loop.

lines.act: ACT THREE — Why pi never ends
lines.text: So if the digits of pi never stop and never loop, pi cannot be a fraction.

lines.act: ACT THREE — Why pi never ends
lines.text: And they don't. This isn't a hunch. It's a theorem.

lines.act: ACT THREE — Why pi never ends
lines.text: In seventeen sixty-one, the Swiss mathematician Johann Heinrich Lambert proved that pi is irrational.

lines.act: ACT THREE — Why pi never ends
lines.text: More than a century later, in eighteen eighty-two, the German mathematician Ferdinand von Lindemann proved something even stronger. Pi is transcendental.

lines.act: ACT THREE — Why pi never ends
lines.text: That means pi is not the solution of any polynomial equation with whole-number coefficients. No finite piece of algebra will ever pin it down.

lines.act: ACT THREE — Why pi never ends
lines.text: You might hope for a simple reason why a number born from a circle has to behave like this.

lines.act: ACT THREE — Why pi never ends
lines.text: Honestly, there isn't a one-line one. The proofs are real, but subtle.

lines.act: ACT THREE — Why pi never ends
lines.text: The shortest, by Ivan Niven in nineteen forty-seven, fits on a single page, but it needs calculus.

lines.act: ACT THREE — Why pi never ends
lines.text: What we can show is what it costs.

lines.act: ACT THREE — Why pi never ends
lines.text: The ancient Greeks asked a famous question. With only a compass and a straight edge, can you draw a square with exactly the same area as a circle?

lines.act: ACT THREE — Why pi never ends
lines.text: For more than two thousand years, people tried. Lindemann's result finally settled it. It is impossible, because pi is transcendental.

lines.act: ACT THREE — Why pi never ends
lines.text: So the endless digits aren't a flaw in the number. They are the reason one of the oldest problems in mathematics could never be solved.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — When the ratio isn't pi
lines.text: Here is something textbooks rarely mention.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — When the ratio isn't pi
lines.text: Pi itself, the number, never changes. It is three point one four one five nine, and so on, forever.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — When the ratio isn't pi
lines.text: But the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter only equals pi on a flat surface.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — When the ratio isn't pi
lines.text: Imagine you are standing on a huge ball, like the Earth. You draw a circle the honest way, by walking the same distance from a centre point in every direction.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — When the ratio isn't pi
lines.text: Now measure around that circle, and divide by its diameter, measured along the ground.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — When the ratio isn't pi
lines.text: You get less than pi. Your diameter had to follow the curve of the ball, so it is longer than it would be on a flat floor, and the ratio shrinks.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — When the ratio isn't pi
lines.text: Push it to the extreme. Put the centre at the North Pole, and let your circle be the equator.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — When the ratio isn't pi
lines.text: The circumference is the whole equator. The diameter runs from the equator, over the pole, and down to the other side. That is half the equator.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — When the ratio isn't pi
lines.text: So the ratio is exactly two.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — When the ratio isn't pi
lines.text: And on a saddle, which curves the other way, the ratio comes out bigger than pi.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — When the ratio isn't pi
lines.text: So the formula you learned, circumference equals pi times diameter, is only true in flat space. Not curving up, not curving down.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — When the ratio isn't pi
lines.text: As far as our best measurements can tell, our universe is flat on the largest scales, to within a fraction of a percent. That's why the school formula works so well for everyday circles.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — When the ratio isn't pi
lines.text: But Einstein's general relativity says that space near heavy objects does curve.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — When the ratio isn't pi
lines.text: Draw a circle around a black hole, and the distance around it no longer matches pi times the distance across.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — When the ratio isn't pi
lines.text: Pi didn't change. The world did.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — When the ratio isn't pi
lines.text: Pi is the constant of flat geometry. When space bends, pi is still there as a number. It just stops describing the circles around you.

lines.act: ACT FIVE — Putting it together
lines.text: So, what is pi, really?

lines.act: ACT FIVE — Putting it together
lines.text: It is not just circumference over diameter. That's the easiest way to measure it, not what it is.

lines.act: ACT FIVE — Putting it together
lines.text: Pi is a limit. It's where the polygons end up as their sides multiply without end, the border between straight and curved.

lines.act: ACT FIVE — Putting it together
lines.text: Pi is the natural measure of turning. Half a turn, on a circle of radius one.

lines.act: ACT FIVE — Putting it together
lines.text: Pi is irrational, and transcendental. Lambert proved the first in seventeen sixty-one, Lindemann the second in eighteen eighty-two, and that is why no compass will ever square the circle.

lines.act: ACT FIVE — Putting it together
lines.text: And pi is the constant of flat space. Bend space, and circles stop obeying it.

lines.act: ACT FIVE — Putting it together
lines.text: Put it all together, and pi is what flat geometry has to say about turning.

lines.act: ACT FIVE — Putting it together
lines.text: Our universe is very nearly flat, which is why pi works so well here, and why it turns up in fields that seem to have nothing to do with circles. Statistics, quantum physics, probability, number theory.

lines.act: ACT FIVE — Putting it together
lines.text: So the next time you see pi in a formula, try this.

lines.act: ACT FIVE — Putting it together
lines.text: There may be no circle anywhere in the problem.

lines.act: ACT FIVE — Putting it together
lines.text: The bell curve of statistics has a square root of pi inside it. Add one, plus a quarter, plus a ninth, plus a sixteenth, on forever, and you get pi squared over six.

lines.act: ACT FIVE — Putting it together
lines.text: But almost always, if you dig, there is a turn, a wave, or a circle hiding somewhere inside the calculation.

lines.act: ACT FIVE — Putting it together
lines.text: Thank you for watching all the way to the end.

lines.act: ACT FIVE — Putting it together
lines.text: If you'll never look at pi quite the same way again, subscribe to ninety-nine percent from scratch, so you don't miss the next one. See you soon.
